title: Extremely Fast and Accurate Transcription with Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC
gist: IBM's Granite team released two compact 470M-parameter English speech-recognition models (Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC) that hit over 12,600 RTFx on an NVIDIA H200 — transcribing 3.5+ hours of speech per second — at 4.85-5.00% aggregate WER, by dropping the LLM decoder for an encoder-only Conformer/CTC design aimed at edge and high-throughput speech-to-text.

insights.claim: IBM's new Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC models are 470M-parameter English ASR models that achieve over 12,600 RTFx aggregate throughput on an NVIDIA H200, transcribing more than 3.5 hours of speech in one second with batched inference.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude throughput gains collapse the cost of bulk transcription — pressure on paid ASR APIs (e.g., transcription SaaS) and a tailwind for on-device/edge speech products.
insights.quote: over 12,600 RTFx on an NVIDIA H200 GPU, meaning they can transcribe more than 3.5 hours of speech in one second using batched inference

insights.claim: The new encoder-only Granite models deliver over 20x faster throughput than previous LM-equipped Granite Speech models while keeping a 470M-parameter memory footprint, at the cost of dropping capabilities like speech translation and keyword biasing.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Signals a bifurcation in speech AI: stripped-down encoder-only models for cheap high-volume transcription vs. LLM-based models for richer tasks — watch where inference spend migrates.
insights.quote: over 20x faster throughput than previous Granite Speech models

insights.claim: IBM shipped a WebGPU browser demo of streaming speech recognition with the Granite Turbo CTC models, running only on Chrome or Edge, demonstrating the models are light enough for client-side inference.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Client-side ASR removes server inference cost entirely for some use cases — a structural threat to per-minute transcription pricing models.

insights.claim: On the OpenASR Leaderboard public English test sets, the noncommercial Granite Turbo CTC model scores 4.85% aggregate WER and the Apache 2.0 model 5.00% WER, with aggregate throughput above 12,600 RTFx — accuracy competitive with far larger models at unprecedented speed.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: The speed-vs-accuracy Pareto frontier for open ASR has moved; incumbents (commercial ASR vendors, larger open models) must now compete on cost per transcribed hour.
insights.quote: the noncommercial model scoring an aggregate 4.85% WER and the Apache 2.0 model scoring 5.00% WER, and unprecedented aggregate throughput in excess of 12,600 RTFx

insights.claim: On the FFASR far-field speech leaderboard as of 25 August 2026, the two Granite Turbo CTC models rank fifth and ninth in accuracy while being the two fastest models listed.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Far-field competence matters for meeting-room, automotive, and smart-device deployments — broadens the addressable market beyond clean-audio transcription.

insights.claim: The noncommercial Granite variant beats the Apache 2.0 variant on most test sets, with a notable edge on SPGI Speech (financial earnings audio) but a noticeable disadvantage on the new chunked Earnings22 test.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: The accuracy gap traces directly to licensing-restricted training data (SPGI, GigaSpeech) — evidence that data licensing, not architecture, is the moat in domain ASR (e.g., earnings-call transcription).

insights.claim: IBM abandoned the acoustic-encoder-plus-projector-plus-LLM-with-LoRA architecture of prior Granite Speech models in favor of a pure encoder-only CTC design for these releases, trading multi-task capability for speed and footprint.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: A counter-trend to bolting LLMs onto everything: for pure transcription, classic encoder/CTC beats LLM pipelines on cost — a template other labs will likely copy for edge ASR.
insights.quote: they are ideal for speech-to-text tasks on edge devices

insights.claim: The key speed unlock in Granite Speech 5.0 is cutting the output token rate from 50 characters per second to 12.5 tokens per second via three stages of 2x temporal subsampling, with strided-convolution downsampling built into the first two of 16 Conformer blocks.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Token-rate reduction is a generalizable efficiency lever for sequence models — expect similar low-frame-rate designs to spread across open ASR, lowering GPU demand per audio-hour.
insights.quote: our previous encoders generated 50 characters per second, the Granite 5.0 models generate 12.5 tokens per second

insights.claim: The models use chunkwise attention specifically to avoid the quadratic scaling of standard dot-product attention with sequence length, plus self-conditioning at the 8th of 16 Conformer blocks, and speech-transcript-trained SentencePiece/BPE tokenizers.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Details how long-audio inference stays cheap and streamable — relevant to anyone modeling inference-cost curves for speech workloads.

insights.claim: IBM released two license-differentiated variants: an Apache 2.0 model trained on ~57,700+ hours of permissive natural data, and a CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 model that adds GigaSpeech (10,000 h) and SPGI Speech (4,900 h) for better accuracy — a deliberate two-tier open-weights licensing strategy.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: The commercial-usable Apache model is the one enterprises can ship; the NC model shows what extra licensed data buys — a live case study of data licensing as the price of accuracy.

insights.claim: IBM trained the models on synthetic data generated with OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss-120b/gpt-oss-20b models and StyleTTS2, including 240 hours of utterances covering numbers, currencies, phone numbers, and addresses.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Open-weight LLMs are now upstream infrastructure in competitors' training pipelines — synthetic targeted data (entities, numerals) is becoming a standard cheap fix for ASR weak spots.

insights.claim: IBM built 2,500 hours of synthetic multi-speaker training data by concatenating single-speaker segments from public corpora (MLS, YODAS, CommonVoice, VoxPopuli, AMI, Earnings-22), targeting multi-speaker and earnings-call-style audio without new data collection.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Cheap synthetic augmentation of public data narrows the gap with proprietary corpora — bearish for the defensibility of pure data-collection plays in speech.

insights.claim: Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC is supported natively in Hugging Face transformers (install from source until the next release), giving IBM immediate distribution through the dominant open-model toolchain.
insights.speaker: Brian Kingsbury
insights.so_what: Day-one transformers integration is the distribution channel that turns model releases into adoption — IBM is competing for open-source speech mindshare against Whisper-class incumbents.
